lessons.title: Lunch Time in the Wild
objectives: Say what common animals eat
Sort animals into plant eaters and meat eaters
explanation: Every animal needs food. Some animals eat only plants — cows eat grass, rabbits eat carrots and leaves, elephants eat leaves and fruit.
Some animals eat other animals — lions, eagles and sharks are hunters.
Some animals eat both plants and animals — bears eat berries and fish; crows eat almost anything!

an animal that eats other animals
what living things eat to grow and have energy

examples: 🐄 A cow eats grass.
🦅 An eagle catches fish and small animals.

story.title: The Picnic Mix-Up
story.text: Momo the bear packed a picnic for friends: grass, carrots, fish and berries. The cow took the grass. The rabbit took the carrots. The eagle took a fish. Momo ate berries AND fish. "I like a bit of everything," Momo smiled.

activities.prompt: Match the animal to its food
Some animals eat plants and meat.

thinking: Why do you think lions don't eat grass?
What do you eat — plants, meat, or both?

lessons.title: The Busy Tree
objectives: Describe how a tree helps many animals
Describe how animals help plants
prerequisites: Knows plants and animals are living
explanation: One tree can be home to many animals. Birds nest in its branches, squirrels store food in it, insects live in its bark, and monkeys eat its fruit.
Animals help trees too. Bees carry pollen so the tree can make fruit. Birds and monkeys eat fruit and drop the seeds far away, where new trees can grow.
When living things help each other like this, everyone does better.

vocabulary.meaning: a safe place
do something useful for someone
with each other

examples: A banyan tree shelters birds, bats and monkeys.
Birds spread seeds of fig trees.

story.title: The Banyan Hotel
story.text: An old banyan tree had many guests. Parrots lived on the top floor, bats hung in the middle, squirrels ran up and down, and ants marched along the roots. "Thank you for your fruit and shade," said the parrots, and they carried its seeds far away so new banyans could grow.

lessons.title: Where Do Fallen Leaves Go?
objectives: Explain what decomposers do
Describe how compost is made
explanation: When leaves fall and plants and animals die, they don't pile up forever. Decomposers break them down into tiny pieces that become part of the soil.
Earthworms, fungi (like mushrooms and mould) and bacteria (tiny living things too small to see) are decomposers.
This is nature's recycling! The nutrients go back into the soil and help new plants grow. People copy this by making compost from vegetable peels.

vocabulary.meaning: a living thing that breaks down dead material
break down slowly
rotted plant waste used to enrich soil
living things like mushrooms and mould

examples: A fallen apple turns brown and soft as it rots.
Mushrooms often grow on dead logs.

story.title: The Leaf Pile Mystery
story.text: Every autumn, Tara's garden was covered in leaves. By spring, they had disappeared! "Who took them?" Tara wondered. She dug a little and found worms, tiny white threads of fungi and dark, crumbly soil. "The decomposers ate them," said Olu, "and gave the soil a gift."

activities.prompt: Mushrooms are a kind of fungus.

thinking: What would the forest look like without decomposers?
Why shouldn't we put plastic in compost?
speaking: Explain nature's recycling to someone using a fallen leaf.

lessons.title: Three Links in a Chain
objectives: Build a three-link food chain
Explain what the arrows mean
explanation: A food chain shows how food passes from one living thing to another. It always starts with a plant, because plants make food from sunlight.
Example: grass → grasshopper → frog. The arrow means "is eaten by". Grass is eaten by the grasshopper, which is eaten by the frog.
Food chains are everywhere: in ponds (algae → tadpole → fish), fields (grass → goat) and gardens (leaf → caterpillar → bird).

vocabulary.meaning: a list showing who eats whom
shows the direction food goes
what living things need to move and grow

examples: Leaf → caterpillar → sparrow.
Seeds → mouse → owl.

story.title: The Pond Party
story.text: In a pond, tiny green algae soaked up sunshine. A tadpole nibbled the algae. A fish gobbled the tadpole. A kingfisher swooped down and caught the fish. "We're a chain," said the kingfisher, "and it all started with sunshine."

activities.prompt: In "leaf → caterpillar → bird", who eats the caterpillar?

thinking: Why does every food chain start with a plant?
What would happen if all the frogs disappeared?
speaking: Make up a food chain from your garden and explain it to someone.

assessment.prompt: Which comes first in a pond food chain?

lessons.title: The Web of Life
objectives: Combine food chains into a food web
Identify producers, consumers, predators and prey
explanation: Most animals eat more than one thing, and are eaten by more than one thing. When food chains join together, they make a food web.
Producers are plants (they make food). Primary consumers eat producers (herbivores). Secondary consumers eat primary consumers. A predator hunts other animals; the animals it hunts are its prey.
In a web, if one species changes, others are affected. If snakes vanished, mice might increase and eat more seeds.

vocabulary.meaning: connected food chains
makes its own food
eats other living things
hunts animals
animals that are hunted

examples: A frog is a predator of insects and prey of snakes.
Grass is eaten by deer, rabbits and grasshoppers.

story.title: The Missing Snakes
story.text: Farmers in a village were scared of snakes and removed many of them. Next season, mice multiplied and ate the grain stores. An old farmer explained: "The snakes were eating the mice. Everything is connected in the web."

activities.prompt: An animal that hunts others is a…
If snakes disappear from a field, mice will probably…
A frog can be both predator and prey.

thinking: Why are food webs more realistic than food chains?
Can removing a predator ever harm the prey species?
speaking: Use a food web drawing to explain to someone what happens if one animal disappears.

assessment.prompt: Changing one species can affect many others in a web.

lessons.title: When Habitats Change
objectives: Describe natural and human causes of habitat change
Explain how living things may respond
explanation: Habitats change. Some changes are natural: seasons, floods, droughts, fires and storms. Many ecosystems recover over time — a burnt grassland can regrow quickly.
Humans also change habitats: building roads and cities, cutting forests, polluting rivers, and draining wetlands.
When a habitat changes, living things might adapt, move somewhere else, or decline. Some species, like crows and pigeons, do well in cities; others, like tigers, need large wild areas.

vocabulary.meaning: when a place where living things live becomes different
harmful substances added to the environment
become fewer
return to a healthy state

examples: A wetland drained for buildings loses its frogs and birds.
Sparrows have declined in some cities as nesting places disappear.

story.title: The Return of the Sparrows
story.text: In one city, people noticed fewer house sparrows. Modern buildings had no gaps for nests. A school club built wooden nest boxes and planted native shrubs. The next spring, chirping returned to the neighbourhood. "Small changes can help," the children realised.

pairs: a river flood after heavy rain

activities.prompt: Which animal often does well in cities?
Some habitats can recover after natural changes.
When their habitat is destroyed, animals may…

thinking: Why do some animals thrive in cities while others disappear?
How can new buildings be designed to help wildlife?
speaking: Describe a change you have noticed in a place near your home and how it affected living things.

revision.notes: Retrieval first, then review notes; interleave with other units; apply in a new example.

lessons.title: Ecological Pyramids
objectives: Explain why energy decreases at each trophic level
Interpret pyramids of numbers and biomass
explanation: Each step in a food chain is a trophic level. When an animal eats, it uses most of the energy to move, keep warm and live; only a small part (often roughly 10%) is stored in its body and passed on.
That's why there is lots of grass, fewer deer and very few tigers: there's less energy available at each higher level.
A pyramid of biomass shows the total mass of living material at each level, usually biggest at the bottom. A pyramid of numbers can have odd shapes — one tree can feed thousands of insects.

vocabulary.meaning: a step in a food chain
the total mass of living material
passing energy from one level to the next
a predator at the top with no natural predators

examples: One tiger may need the energy of many deer over a year, which need huge amounts of plants.
A single banyan supports thousands of insects: an inverted number pyramid.

story.title: Why So Few Tigers?
story.text: Kiko asked, "Why are there millions of insects but only a few tigers?" Nova drew a pyramid: wide grass at the bottom, fewer deer above, and a tiny tiger at the top. "At every step, most of the energy is used up living," Nova explained. "There's only enough left at the top for a few."

activities.prompt: At each trophic level, the energy passed on is usually…
Why are there fewer top predators?
options: less energy is available at higher levels

activities.prompt: A pyramid of biomass is usually widest at the bottom.

thinking: Why might eating more plants and fewer animals feed more people with the same land?
Why can a pyramid of numbers be upside-down?
speaking: Explain an energy pyramid to someone using building blocks.

project.title: Energy Pyramid Model

assessment.prompt: Grass is at which trophic level?

lessons.title: The Carbon Cycle
objectives: Describe the main processes of the carbon cycle
Explain how humans affect it
explanation: Carbon is in all living things. Plants take in carbon dioxide from the air during photosynthesis and build it into their bodies. Animals get carbon by eating plants.

Living things release carbon dioxide back into the air through respiration. Decomposers release carbon when they break down dead things. Burning wood or fossil fuels (combustion) also releases carbon dioxide.
Fossil fuels are ancient carbon stores. Burning them quickly adds carbon dioxide to the air faster than plants and oceans can absorb it.

vocabulary.meaning: the movement of carbon between living things, air, land and oceans
releasing energy from food, giving out carbon dioxide
burning
coal, oil or gas from ancient living things

examples: A tree trunk is mostly made from carbon taken from the air.
Your breath contains carbon dioxide from respiration.

story.title: The Journey of a Carbon Atom
story.text: A carbon atom floated in the air as carbon dioxide. A mango leaf captured it. It became part of a mango, which Kiko ate. Kiko breathed it out again. It drifted over the ocean, dissolved, and was built into a tiny shell. Millions of years later, it was part of a rock. Carbon never stops travelling.

activities.prompt: Match the process to what it does to carbon dioxide in the air

thinking: How could planting trees help balance the carbon cycle?
Why is burning fossil fuels different from breathing?
speaking: Tell the story of a carbon atom's journey to someone.

project.title: Carbon Cycle Board Game

Play and track your carbon atom
Discuss which stations held carbon longest

assessment.prompt: Which process adds CO₂ to the air?
Carbon moves between living things and the environment.

lessons.title: Trophic Cascades
objectives: Explain keystone species and trophic cascades
Evaluate evidence from real case studies
prerequisites: Understands food webs and energy flow
explanation: A keystone species has a much bigger effect on its ecosystem than its numbers suggest — removing it causes big changes. Top predators like tigers and wolves are often keystone species.

A trophic cascade happens when changes at one level ripple down the food web. When wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone (USA) in 1995, elk behaviour and numbers changed; in some areas, willow and aspen recovered. Scientists still debate how strong the cascade was.
Ecosystem engineers physically shape habitats: elephants push over trees and open grasslands, and their dung spreads seeds. In India, elephants and hornbills are key seed dispersers.

context.text: Ecologists agree wolves affected Yellowstone's ecosystem but debate how much plant recovery was due to wolves versus other factors like climate and other predators.

vocabulary.meaning: a species with a disproportionately large effect on its ecosystem
ripple effects through food web levels
a species that physically changes its habitat
returning a species to an area it had vanished from

examples: Sea otters eat sea urchins, protecting kelp forests.
Hornbills spread seeds of large forest trees.

story.title: The Wolves Return
story.text: For 70 years, Yellowstone had no wolves, and elk grazed riverbanks bare. In 1995 wolves were brought back. Elk became warier and moved more; in some places young willows began to grow again. Scientists collected decades of data — and discovered that ecosystems are more connected, and more complicated, than anyone expected.

options: has a big effect on its ecosystem

activities.prompt: Removing a top predator can cause…
Scientists fully agree on every detail of the Yellowstone story.
Match the species to its role

thinking: Why should we be careful about simple "one cause" stories in ecology?
Which animal might be a keystone species near where you live?
speaking: Explain the Yellowstone story to someone, including what scientists still debate.

project.title: Keystone Case Study Report

assessment.prompt: Wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone in…

revision.notes: Self-test, explain the reasoning aloud, connect to other subjects, and attempt a transfer problem.

lessons.title: What Nature Does for Us
objectives: Classify ecosystem services
Explain the value of mangroves and wetlands
explanation: Ecosystem services are benefits people get from nature. Provisioning services give products: food, timber, medicines, fresh water. Regulating services control natural processes: pollination, flood control, climate regulation, water purification.
Cultural services are non-material: recreation, beauty, spiritual and educational value. Supporting services make the others possible: soil formation, nutrient cycling, photosynthesis.
Mangroves, like the Sundarbans, protect coasts from storm surges, nurture fish nurseries and store carbon. Wetlands like East Kolkata Wetlands naturally treat wastewater and support fisheries.

context.text: The East Kolkata Wetlands, a Ramsar site, use sewage-fed fisheries and natural processes to treat a large share of the city's wastewater.

vocabulary.meaning: a benefit people get from nature
providing products
controlling natural processes
a wetland of international importance

examples: Bees pollinating crops: regulating service.
A sacred grove's spiritual value: cultural service.

story.title: The Mangrove Shield
story.text: When a powerful cyclone struck a stretch of coast, villages behind thick mangrove forests generally suffered less damage than those where mangroves had been cleared for farms. Fishermen began replanting mangroves — they had learned what the forest did for them.

activities.prompt: A wetland of international importance is a…

thinking: Should we put a money value on nature? What are the risks and benefits?
Which ecosystem service do you rely on most every day?
speaking: Give a short talk convincing your local council to protect a wetland or park.

project.title: Ecosystem Services Map

assessment.prompt: Cultural services include beauty and recreation.

units.title: Population Ecology
units.summary: How populations grow and are limited.
objectives: Describe exponential and logistic growth
Interpret predator–prey cycles
masteryCriteria: Applies limiting factors to real cases

revision.notes: Spaced retrieval with written explanations, peer-teaching, and an extension question each cycle.

lessons.title: Carrying Capacity
objectives: Describe exponential and logistic growth
Interpret predator–prey cycles
explanation: With unlimited resources, a population can grow exponentially — doubling repeatedly. Bacteria in a fresh nutrient dish can do this for a while.

Real environments have limits: food, space, water, predators and disease. As a population approaches the carrying capacity (K) — the maximum the environment can support long-term — growth slows, producing an S-shaped (logistic) curve.

Predator and prey populations often cycle: more prey allows predators to increase; more predators reduce prey; fewer prey then reduce predators. Historical fur-trapping records of Canadian lynx and snowshoe hare are a classic example.

vocabulary.meaning: the maximum population an environment can sustain
growth by repeated multiplication
S-shaped growth levelling off at carrying capacity
a resource that restricts growth

examples: Locust swarms can grow explosively after rains.
An island deer population crashing after overgrazing.

story.title: The Island Deer
story.text: A few reindeer were introduced to St. Matthew Island in Alaska in 1944 with no predators. Their numbers rose to about 6,000 by 1963 — then they ate the lichen faster than it could regrow. After a harsh winter, the population crashed to a few dozen. The island had a carrying capacity, and they overshot it.

options: logistic growth levelling at carrying capacity

activities.prompt: Predator and prey populations can rise and fall in cycles.

thinking: Does the idea of carrying capacity apply to humans? How might technology change it?
Why might predator peaks lag behind prey peaks?
speaking: Explain the St. Matthew Island story using a graph you draw.

project.title: Yeast Population Experiment
steps: Mix yeast with different sugar amounts in bottles
Fit balloons and measure their circumference every 15 minutes
Graph the results
Relate the curve shape to carrying capacity and limiting factors

assessment.prompt: Overshooting carrying capacity can cause a population crash.

mastery: Applies limiting factors to real cases

revision.notes: Spaced retrieval with written explanations, peer-teaching, and an extension question each cycle.

lessons.title: Measuring Biodiversity
objectives: Calculate and interpret a simple diversity index
Analyse causes of and responses to biodiversity loss
explanation: Biodiversity includes species richness (how many species) and evenness (how balanced their numbers are). Two meadows with ten species each can differ if one is dominated by a single species.
Simpson's index of diversity (1 − Σn(n−1)/N(N−1)) gives a value from 0 to 1: higher means more diverse. Ecologists sample with quadrats and transects to estimate it.

Major drivers of biodiversity loss are land-use change, overexploitation, climate change, pollution and invasive species. Global agreements, such as the 2022 Kunming-Montreal framework, include a target to conserve 30% of land and sea by 2030.

context.text: The IPBES 2019 global assessment estimated around one million species are threatened with extinction, many within decades, without action.

vocabulary.meaning: the number of different species
how evenly individuals are spread among species
a number summarising richness and evenness
a non-native species that spreads and causes harm

examples: Lantana is an invasive shrub in many Indian forests.
A transect samples species along a line across changing habitats.

story.title: Two Meadows
story.text: Two student teams each found 8 plant species in their meadow. "Same diversity!" they said. But in one meadow, 90% of plants were a single grass. Calculating Simpson's index showed the other meadow was much more diverse. Counting species alone had hidden the difference.

activities.prompt: Simpson's index of diversity close to 1 means…
Lantana is an invasive species in parts of India.
A "30 by 30" target aims to conserve…

thinking: Why is evenness important, not just the number of species?
Who should pay for protecting biodiversity in poorer regions?
speaking: Present your biodiversity survey results and what they suggest about the habitat.

steps: Sample 5 quadrats in two different areas (lawn vs wild patch)
